segments.voice: Yesterday in Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum: jagarana, the vigil, kept awake together, and the one who starts the song. Did you lift someone who was flagging? Today, what fills the long hours. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-seven.

Rough brown beads, a little uneven, each one wrinkled like a tiny walnut. They hang from the fingers of a woman sitting against a pillar, and they move. The thumb draws one bead toward the palm, her lips move, and the next bead comes. Then the next. She isn't reading anything. She isn't singing with the crowd right now. She's saying one short phrase, once per bead, and has been for a long while. Around her the night goes on, songs rising and falling, the line to the shrine moving and stopping. Her beads keep their own slow time. The first lessons of the night were a resolve, a fast and the will to stay awake. Today's lesson is what you hold onto once you're up.
screen: `ROUGH BROWN BEADS.` → `ONE PHRASE PER BEAD.` → `WHAT YOU HOLD ONCE YOU'RE UP.`

segments.voice: The phrase is Om Namah Shivaya. Namah Shivaya is the Panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra: na, mah, shi, va, ya. And you've already met it this year. It's the line from deep inside the Rudram, salutation to Shiva, the kind one. The great Vedic hymn and the bead in a tired hand are joined by those five syllables. Saying a mantra over and over like this is called japa, and the Shiva Purana praises this five-syllable mantra at length. Here's why it suits this night. A long night needs something small. At ten in the evening a long hymn is easy to follow. At three in the morning, that gets hard. But you can still hold five syllables. Japa is built for exactly the hour when bigger things slip away. It can be said aloud, whispered, or held silently in the mind, so it works in a loud crowd and in a quiet room. The beads matter too. They're rudraksha, and the Shiva Purana tells that these seeds came from Shiva's own tears. The beads do something practical: they keep count, so the mind doesn't have to, and they give the hand a job, so the body stays in the practice when the thoughts wander off. When you notice you've drifted, there's a bead in your fingers, waiting. So the night curriculum's fourth lesson is a thread. Through all the hours, all the songs and the waiting, one short name keeps running, the same name the Rudram bowed to. The night is long. The thread is short enough to hold.
screen: `NAMAH SHIVAYA: FIVE SYLLABLES.` · `THE LINE FROM INSIDE THE RUDRAM.` · `JAPA: SMALL ENOUGH FOR 3 A.M.` · `RUDRAKSHA: BEADS FROM SHIVA'S TEARS.` · then, large: `A THREAD SHORT ENOUGH TO HOLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a thread through the sit. Settle, and breathe. Choose something short to repeat, one breath at a time. If you pray, you can use Om Namah Shivaya, or a name of God from your own tradition. If you don't, a single word will do, or simply counting breaths from one to ten and starting again. If you have beads, or even a string with knots, let the fingers move one at a time. When you notice you've drifted, don't start over in your head. Just take the next bead, the next breath, the next word. The bell holds the time.
Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum. Lesson four: japa, the name repeated through the night, Om Namah Shivaya, a thread short enough to hold at three in the morning.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri, some who keep the vigil do japa of Om Namah Shivaya, aloud, whispered or silently, counting on a rudraksha mala, alongside temple songs and worship through the night.
